newsitem.title: UK: Mexico economic policy seen steady after election.
newsitem.headline: Mexico economic policy seen steady after election.

text.p: Mexico's economic policy is widely expected to continue on track despite a dramatic shift in the political landscape after the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party's (PRI) election upset, financial analysts in London said on Monday. Emerging market experts said the fairness of the election, unlike the impression after previous elections, would be seen as a watershed event in Mexican politics and should have a positive effect for investment prospects over the longer term.
"There are lots of positive elements in this, particularly that it shows democracy is now functioning well in Mexico," said Peter West, chief economist at BBV Latinvest.

Indeed, Mexican Brady bond prices rallied following the news, with pars MX625L19=RR rising 1/2 to 80 bid, discount bonds MXFLL19=RR gaining 1/4 to 94-1/8 bid and UMS-26 MXUMS=RR firming 1/2 to 117-1/4 bid.

Emerging market experts also applauded comments by Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo, who congratulated the PRI opposition candidate Cuauhtemoc Cardenas of the Party of the Democratic Revolution on winning the first mayoral election in Mexico City.

Preliminary results showed that the PRI lost its majority in the Chamber of Deputies for the first time in its 68-year history and was trounced by a left wing opponent in Mexico City's first ever mayoral elections.

"Mexico has come a long way to becoming a fully Westernized democracy. Zedillo's comments can only add to authenticity of the results and it only confirms there won't be any major shift in policy as a result of this," said Chris Portman, senior economist at ANZ Investment in London.
Still, analysts said any backlash within the PRI could add uncertainty over how economic policies are implemented.
"If the (RPI) dinosaurs were to take this badly, that would be a danger," said West.

Richard Gray, emerging market analyst at Bank America, agreed, saying he was concerned PRI hardliners might now conclude they have lost ground because of the absence of the "feel good factor" in the domestic economy.

"There is quite a lot of success to report on Mexico but most of it has been in the export sector of the economy. What the old guard will now claim is that there must be a faster rate of translation from that export success to the domestic side and this is my concern going forward," said Gray.
Gray added he was concerned the PRI's loss could trigger a relaxation in fiscal and monetary policies.
Another uncertainty, analysts said, is how the PRI will handle negotiations with other parties in Congress.

"It is a different environment so that will generate some uncertainty. The big change with the PRI losing control is that they will have to negotiate certain things which they never had to do before," said West, who noted that the annual budget would be of particular interest.
Analysts said the fairness of the elections would be viewed positively by the rating agencies although an immediate upgrade was unlikely.

"I don't think it (a ratings upgrade) will come immediately but I think the mere fact the elections have gone off without any major hitch can only be positive in the long-term for any ratings upgrade," said West of BBV Latinvest.

However, West said the rating agencies were likely to wait to make sure that nothing unforeseen happened. "The ratings agencies came close to upgrading Mexico before the devaluation so I think they will proceed with caution if nothing else.".
Currently, Mexico is rated BB by Standard and Poor's Corp with a stable outlook, Ba2 by Moody's Investors Service Inc and BB by European rating agency IBCA.
Earlier today, IBCA said it was continuing to monitor the Mexican elections and added that progress had been made.
